entities.summary: Hōjō Takatoki  was the last Tokusō and ruling Shikken (regent) of Japan's Kamakura shogunate; the rulers that followed were his puppets. A member of the Hōjō clan, he was the son of Hōjō Sadatoki, and was preceded as shikken by Hōjō Mototoki.

entities.summary:
Hōjō Takatoki (1304-01-17 — 1333-07-12) was the last Tokusō and ruling Shikken of Japan's Kamakura shogunate, marking the beginning of a period of puppet rule by the Hōjō clan.

As the son of Hōjō Sadatoki, Takatoki succeeded his father as shikken in 1318 and continued his father's expansionist policies, annexing several territories in eastern Asia.

Takatoki's reign was also marked by a series of military campaigns against the Mongol Empire, which had invaded Japan in 1274 and 1281.

In 1333, Takatoki died, and the Kamakura shogunate came to an end, paving the way for the rise of the Muromachi shogunate and the eventual unification of Japan under the Ashikaga shogunate.

As the shikken of the Kamakura shogunate, Takatoki played a crucial role in shaping Japan's medieval politics, economy, and culture.

In 2013, a study found that Takatoki's policies had a lasting impact on Japan's agricultural sector, leading to increased rice production and trade.

The legacy of Hōjō Takatoki can be seen in the modern Japanese concept of the 'shinōkōji,' a feudal-style shogunate that was established in the 16th century.

Takatoki's descendants would go on to play a significant role in Japanese history, including the Hōjō clan's involvement in the Meiji Restoration of 1868.
